claims.claim: The dominant industrial model is linear: materials are extracted, made into products, used, and discarded as waste ('take-make-waste'); a circular economy is defined in contrast to it.
The Ellen MacArthur Foundation frames the circular economy around three principles: eliminate waste and pollution, circulate products and materials (at their highest value), and regenerate nature.

The butterfly diagram distinguishes a technical cycle (durable materials such as metals and plastics kept in use through reuse, repair, remanufacture, and recycling) from a biological cycle (biodegradable materials returned to the biosphere via composting and anaerobic digestion).

Keeping a product in use through the inner loops (reuse, repair, refurbishment, remanufacture) generally retains more value and uses less energy than recycling, because recycling typically degrades material quality; recycling is the last resort among the R strategies.

A common academic framing, the 9R framework, orders strategies as Refuse, Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Refurbish, Remanufacture, Repurpose, Recycle, Recover; tighter (lower-numbered) loops require fewer external inputs and are considered more circular.

U.S. law defines a circular economy: the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act (enacted December 18, 2020) defines it as a systems-focused approach involving processes that are restorative or regenerative by design, maintain resources at their highest value for as long as possible, and aim to eliminate waste through superior design of materials, products, and systems.

EPA describes a circular economy as one that reduces material use, redesigns materials and products to be less resource intensive, and recovers material or energy from waste; its Circular Economy Strategy Series includes the National Recycling Strategy plus strategies on plastic pollution and on food waste and organics.

Global material extraction rose from about 30 billion tonnes in 1970 to 106 billion tonnes in 2024-era estimates, roughly tripling in five decades, and is projected to rise about 60 percent by 2060 (UNEP International Resource Panel, Global Resources Outlook 2024).

The share of secondary (recycled/recirculated) materials in the global economy fell from 9.1% in 2018 to 7.2% in 2023, indicating that measured global circularity is low and declining even as the concept spreads (Circularity Gap Report 2024, Circle Economy Foundation).

Circular business models shift value from selling more units toward keeping products and materials in circulation: product-as-a-service (leasing/performance contracts), sharing platforms, and take-back/reverse-logistics schemes.

'Circular' is aspirational: perfect closed loops are not achievable because materials dissipate and degrade, so circularity is a direction of travel measured by how much material is kept in use, not an achievable end state of zero extraction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much of the economy is 'circular' and whether progress is being made
positions: The circular economy is entering the mainstream and adoption discussion is rising rapidly (Circle Economy, EMF).
Measured global circularity fell from 9.1% (2018) to 7.2% (2023), so material-use trends are moving the wrong way (Circularity Gap Report 2024).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported by the same source community: interest and policy activity are growing while the physical metric declines because total extraction keeps rising faster than recirculation. The lesson presents the metric as low and declining, dated to 2023, and treats circularity as a direction rather than an achieved state.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft treated 'circular economy' as a generic study-skills concept ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'organize information') with no environmental content, no principles, no cycles, and no data. None of that is substantive and all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual concept: linear vs circular, the three EMF principles, the R-ladder, technical/biological cycles, business models, and the honest low-circularity caveat.
Added dated quantitative anchors (7.2% global circularity in 2023; 106 billion tonnes material use; ~60% projected rise by 2060).
Added the U.S. statutory definition and EPA framing.
rightsIssues: Ellen MacArthur Foundation content is REFERENCE_ONLY: its principles and butterfly diagram are attributed and described, and no EMF wording is reproduced verbatim beyond short definitional phrases attributed to it.
